hints: Start from cobalt metal, atomic number 27 with configuration $[Ar] 3d^7 4s^2$, and remember which subshell loses electrons first when a positive ion forms.
walkthrough:
Build from the cobalt atom**
Cobalt has atomic number 27, so the neutral atom is $[Ar] 3d^7 4s^2$. Think of $[Ar]$ as shorthand for everything up to argon, then you add the outer electrons.

Remove 4s electrons first**
This is the classic trap. When a d block metal ionises, the $4s$ electrons are always lost before the $3d$ electrons, even though $4s$ fills first. So $\text{Co}^{2+}$ loses the two $4s$ electrons to leave $[Ar] 3d^7$. $\text{Co}^{3+}$ loses the two $4s$ electrons plus one $3d$ electron to leave $[Ar] 3d^6$.

hints: Compare $E^{\ominus}$ values directly, the more positive half equation takes electrons and is reduced while the less positive half equation runs in reverse and is oxidised.
Think about what species in an aqueous solution left open to air could be oxidised by a very strong oxidant with $E^{\ominus} = +1.82$ V, focusing on water forming $\text{O}_2$.

Now repeat the comparison for $[\text{Co(edta)}]^{-}$ with $E^{\ominus} = +0.38$ V against the $\text{O}_2$ to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ value of +1.23 V and decide if oxidation of water is still feasible.
walkthrough:
Use $E^{\ominus}$ as a competition for electrons**
Picture two half equations competing. The one with the more positive $E^{\ominus}$ wins electrons and gets reduced, forcing the other to run backwards and get oxidised. That is all you need to predict feasibility.

Test free $\text{Co}^{3+}$ against water**
$$\text{Co}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Co}^{2+} \quad E^{\ominus} = +1.82\ \text{V}$$
$$\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^{+} + 4\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \quad E^{\ominus} = +1.23\ \text{V}$$
+1.82 V is clearly greater than +1.23 V, so $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is the stronger oxidant. It takes electrons from water, so $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is reduced to $\text{Co}^{2+}$ while water is oxidised: $2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^{+} + 4\text{e}^{-}$. You would see bubbles of $\text{O}_2$ gas evolve.

Test the edta complex against water**
$$[\text{Co(edta)}]^{-} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons [\text{Co(edta)}]^{2-} \quad E^{\ominus} = +0.38\ \text{V}$$
Now +0.38 V is much less positive than +1.23 V. The water half equation now wins, so water cannot be oxidised by $[\text{Co(edta)}]^{-}$. Complexing with $\text{edta}^{4-}$ has hugely stabilised cobalt(III) relative to cobalt(II). So the solution is stable in air with no change.

Final answer: aqueous solution of $\text{Co}^{3+}$: $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is reduced to $\text{Co}^{2+}$ with evolution of $\text{O}_2$ from oxidation of water, since $E^{\ominus}(\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}) = +1.82$ V is more positive than $E^{\ominus}(\text{O}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}) = +1.23$ V.
aqueous solution of $[\text{Co(edta)}]^{-}$: no change / reaction not feasible, since $E^{\ominus} = +0.38$ V is less positive than for $\text{O}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Recall what gentle heating does first to a hexahydrate, think about steam condensing as colourless droplets on the cool upper walls of the tube.
Recall how magnesium nitrate decomposes on strong heating to the oxide plus $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$, and think about the colour of $\text{NO}_2$ and the test for $\text{O}_2$.
walkthrough:
Gentle heating drives off water of crystallisation**
$\text{Co}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ contains a lot of water. On gentle warming that water is released as steam, which cools and condenses as colourless droplets higher up the boiling tube. The red crystals will appear to dissolve in their own water of crystallisation, turning to a liquid or solution.

Strong heating decomposes the nitrate like magnesium nitrate**
Magnesium nitrate gives: $2\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$. Cobalt(II) nitrate behaves the same way, forming the oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen. So expect dense brown fumes of $\text{NO}_2$ gas and colourless $\text{O}_2$ gas that relights a glowing splint. Any two clear visual observations earn the marks.

Final answer: Any two of: steam evolved forming condensation / droplets on cool part of tube and red solid dissolves / forms solution; on stronger heating brown fumes of $\text{NO}_2$ evolved; $\text{O}_2$ evolved which relights a glowing splint.

hints: Focus on how the size of the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ion changes from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and what this means for charge density.
Link high charge density to the ability of the cation to distort the electron cloud of the large $\text{NO}_3^{-}$ ion and weaken the N to O bond, making decomposition easier.
walkthrough:
Track cation size down the group**
All Group 2 ions carry the same 2+ charge, but the ionic radius increases from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ down to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ as extra electron shells are added. Larger ion with the same charge means lower charge density.

Connect polarising power to nitrate stability**
Decomposition happens because the positive $\text{M}^{2+}$ ion pulls on the electron cloud of the $\text{NO}_3^{-}$ ion and distorts it, weakening the N to O bond so it breaks more easily to give $\text{NO}_2$ plus $\text{O}^{2-}$. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion is strongly polarising and distorts $\text{NO}_3^{-}$ a lot, so decomposition is easy. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ion polarises $\text{NO}_3^{-}$ much less, the nitrate ion stays more stable, so a higher temperature is needed. Hence thermal stability increases down the group.

Final answer: Down Group 2 the cationic radius / size of $\text{M}^{2+}$ increases.
Charge density and polarising power decrease, so there is less distortion / polarisation of the $\text{NO}_3^{-}$ ion, the N to O bond is weakened less and more heat is needed to decompose the nitrate.
